text: He came to the door months ago, thin and frightened, a slave from the province of Asia who had run from his master. In a city of a million people he could have vanished. Instead he found his way to the one prisoner in Rome who knew his master’s name.
Scripture does not tell us what Philemon did. But the letter was kept, and copied, and read in the churches ever since.
Tychicus carried Paul’s letter to the Colossians, traveling with Onesimus, whom Paul called a faithful and beloved brother from their own town (Colossians 4:7–9).
Partway through, Paul takes the pen from you and writes the next lines himself, slowly, in large letters, the chain clinking against the table.
The closer you get to the Lycus valley, the less Onesimus says. On the last night he asks you, very quietly, what happens to runaways. You tell him the truth. Then you tell him what Paul wrote.
The whole church is gathered in Philemon’s house, and Onesimus is standing at the door. You are to read the letter. Where do you stand?
Since then he has learned the Way, been baptized, and made himself so useful that Paul calls him his own heart. And Roman law says he must go back.
No one speaks. Philemon stands for a long time, looking at the young man in the doorway who once ran from him. Then he crosses the room.

I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love, and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints; that the fellowship of your faith may become effective, in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus. For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.

Therefore, though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate, yet for love’s sake I rather beg, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I beg you for my child, whom I have become the father of in my chains, Onesimus, who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me. I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart,

whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News. But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will. For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker, to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus, our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, put that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).
I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).

Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord. Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say. Also, prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.

I beg you for my child, whom I have become the father of in my chains, Onesimus, who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me. I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart,
Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.
